narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 71.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades had the strongest negative impact. Placing in the second decile is substantially below the average of sixth decile among students who were accepted, and this early performance strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Your third-year grades were the second most influential factor; ranking in the third decile again fell short of the roughly sixth-decile average for accepted students and further increased the predicted risk of failing the bar. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.80, compared with an average of 3.23 among accepted applicants, added a smaller but still noticeable push in the same direction.

Although your high family income, LSAT score of 35, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in the outcome, the model concluded that your academic record in college made success on the bar exam less likely than the school is willing to accept.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retake challenging courses to raise your GPA, seek structured academic support, and consider delaying re-application until you have a clearer record of improved performance. Many students successfully reapply after addressing these exact weaknesses.
